sources.title: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Quality Assurance Practices and Gaps ...
sources.text: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly used in software engineering, web automation, research assistance, personal productivity, and other domains. By integrating LLMs with planning, memory, retrieval, tool use, code execution, and interaction with the external environment, these agents can perform complex tasks with increasing autonomy. However, this autonomy also introduces new reliability, safety, and security risks, creating a need for systematic quality assurance (QA) practices tailored to agentic systems. In this paper, we present a large-scale empirical study of QA practices in 157 open-source LLM-based agent projects, each with at least 100 GitHub stars. We analyze repository documentation, source code, configuration files, tests, and structured review evidence to characterize how current projects address QA practices across four layers: execution surfaces, safeguards, testing artifacts, risk scenarios, and recurring QA gaps. Our results show that existing QA practices primarily focus on validating basic functionality and constraining high-risk actions. However, coverage remains fragmented across the four layers: the breadth of execution surfaces makes QA coverage difficult to trace, controls are not always applied consistently across equivalent routes, tests rarely target boundary, adversarial, or multi-step tool-use failures, and potential risk scenarios are seldom translated into end-to-end QA checks. Overall, our findings show that current agent QA practices provide only partial protection against high-risk agent actions and do not consistently ensure that model-influenced behavior is bounded across all execution surfaces. We argue that agent QA should move beyond feature-level checks toward end-to-end validation of whether agent workflows remain within intended boundaries when they combine untrusted inputs, model decisions, tools, persistent state, and external APIs. Large language model (LLM)-based agents are rapidly changing how software systems are designed, developed, and used [ 1 , 2 ] . Unlike traditional LLM applications that primarily return direct responses, agents combine models with planning, memory, tool use, code execution, retrieval, browser interaction, file manipulation, and external services [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . These capabilities support multi-step autonomy across software engineering [ 7 , 8 ] , browser and computer automation [ 9 ] , research assistance [ 1 , 2 ] , and security-oriented evaluation [ 10 , 11 ] . This shift creates a quality-assurance challenge beyond response correctness. A conventional LLM application may produce an incorrect answer, a hallucinated explanation, or a misleading recommendation. An agent may instead execute shell commands, modify files, browse websites, call APIs, install packages, or delegate tasks to subagents. Model outputs can therefore influence external actions [ 10 , 9 , 11 ] , with consequences such as corrupted files, privacy leakage, unsafe commands, insecure dependency installation, financial loss, compromised credentials, or harmful third-party interactions [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] . Agent QA must therefore ask whether model-influenced actions are bounded across interaction and execution surfaces. Despite the rapid evolution of LLM-based agents and the growing body of work on agent architectures, benchmarks, and security, little is known about how quality assurance is actually engineered in the wild. It remains unclear which QA practices developers adopt, how safeguards and testing are integrated across different execution paths, and whether current repositories provide evidence of end-to-end assurance for model-mediated actions. Open-source repositories provide a unique opportunity to study these engineering practices because they expose testing infrastructure, safeguard implementations, configuration files, documentation, evaluation scripts, and deployment artifacts that collectively reflect observable QA activities during development. To fill this gap, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of 157 open-source LLM-based agent projects, systematically characterizing repository-visible QA practices across architecture, execution surfaces, safeguards, testing artifacts, and risk scenarios. The corpus spans SWE automation (26.8%), personal and multichannel assistants (19.7%), coding assistants (19.1%), research and information agents (13.4%), browser/computer-use automation (12.1%), and domain-specific agents (8.9%). Because LLM-based agent behavior emerges from interactions among reasoning, planning, execution interfaces, external tools, and runtime safeguards, QA cannot be evaluated solely by inspecting the model outputs. Instead, it must consider how actions are introduced into architecture, exposed through execution surfaces, constrained by safeguards, validated through testing, and connected through potential risk scenarios. We therefore analyze repository-visible QA practices across four layers: execution surfaces , safeguards , testing artifacts , and risk scenarios . For each layer, we code what the repository makes inspectable, including action routes, controls, tests, and risk chains. These codes indicate visible QA practices in the repository; they do not show that a mechanism is effective after deployment. Section III defines the coding rubric and review process. Through this analysis, we identify recurring QA practices and uncover important QA gaps across the model-to-action workflow. Our results show that agent projects often expose broad execution surfaces and include controls such as approval, sandboxing, permission checks, redaction, and domain scoping. However, these controls are not always applied consistently across equivalent routes. Agent-specific tests for boundary, adversarial, or multi-step tool-use failures remain rare. The risk scenarios we report should therefore be read as candidate model-to-action situations that need boundary review, not as confirmed vulnerabilities. These findings suggest that QA for agents should extend beyond model-output correctness to systematic reasoning about the complete model-to-action workflow. In addition to asking whether the model gives the right answer, agent QA should ask whether model-influenced actions remain authorized, scoped, monitored, and tested when they pass through tools, plugins, browser state, permissions, runtime execution, and user-facing paths. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the background and related work. Section III presents the methodology and empirical study design. Section IV reports the results. Section V discusses threats to validity, and Section VI concludes the paper. Data Availability: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Quality-Assurance-Practices-and-Gaps-in-AI-Agents-85F2/ LLM-based agents combine model inference with memory, planning, tools, perception, and cooperation [ 1 , 2 ] . Prior work has introduced core patterns such as ReAct-style reasoning and acting [ 3 ] , MRKL-style tool routing [ 4 ] , reflection and search-based agents [ 5 , 16 , 17 ] , memory-centered agents [ 18 , 19 ] , and multi-agent coordination frameworks [ 6 , 20 , 7 , 8 ] . These architectures are usually discussed as capability mechanisms, but they also define trust boundaries: ReAct loops repeatedly mix observations with actions, tool routers map model decisions to external functions, memory systems persist prior context, and multi-agent systems delegate work across roles or workers. We use this literature to code repository architecture, but our focus is narrower: how these architectures expose and constrain safety- and security-relevant execution paths in real projects. Prior security work motivates this focus. Prompt-injection studies show that untrusted content can redirect model behavior, especially when webpages, documents, emails, issues, or repository files enter agent context [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . This risk becomes more concrete in agents because injected instructions can be followed by tool calls, file access, browser actions, or API requests. Agent benchmarks such as ToolEmu, AgentDojo, and Agent Security Bench evaluate attacks and defenses in tool-using environments [ 10 , 9 , 11 ] , while OWASP’s LLM guidance highlights prompt injection, excessive agency, insecure output handling, sensitive information disclosure, and supply-chain risk [ 15 ] . Recent MCP and secure-agent studies further examine MCP security, capability-oriented defenses, and cross-tool state leakage or pollution [ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] . Together, these works identify important risk classes, but they do not directly measure how often open-source agent repositories expose the corresponding tools, policies, tests, and configuration paths. Empirical OSS security research mines repositories, packages, and static-analysis warnings to understand security practice in the wild [ 25 , 26 ] ; recent agent-testing work studies developer-written test functions across agent frameworks and applications [ 27 ] . Our study complements this body of work by providing a repository-level perspective on how QA is engineered in practice. Whereas prior work primarily evaluates agent capabilities, benchmark performance, or individual attacks, our study systematically analyzes repository-visible engineering artifacts that provide evidence of QA in open-source LLM-based agents. We take a broader view in which tests are one evidence source alongside code, configuration, documentation, safeguards, execution surfaces, and structured risk observations. This distinction matters because a repository may document a safeguard without testing it, test a permission component without applying it to every interface, or expose a risky surface without containing a confirmed vulnerability. Figure 1 illustrates the overall workflow of our study, which consists of three stages: repository selection, repository review and annotation, and cross-repository synthesis. During the review stage, we apply a four-layer coding rubric, developed from the literature reviewed in Section II and our initial exploration of selected repositories, to annotate repository artifacts as execution-surface, safeguard, testing-artifact, and risk-scenario records. These layers separate where agents can act, how actions are controlled, how behavior is tested, and which situations require boundary review. During the synthesis stage, we aggregate these coded records to derive corpus-level statistics, QA practice families, and undercovered QA problems. To avoid ambiguity, we use three terms consistently. Repository artifacts are the inspected sources, including documentation, source code, configuration files, manifests, tests, examples, and deployment artifacts. Coded records are the structured annotations derived from those artifacts, such as execution-surface records, safeguard records, testing-artifact records, and risk-scenario records. Analysis layers are the four categories used to organize those records: execution surfaces, safeguards, testing artifacts, and risk scenarios. For our analysis, we target popular LLM-based agent applications whose repositories provide enough artifacts to examine QA-relevant behavior and contain executable entry points or package manifests. We focus on public GitHub projects with at least 100 stars as of May 2026, so that the corpus reflects actively visible projects with enough adoption and repository artifacts for systematic review. We first collected candidate repositories using agent-focused search terms, including “AI agent”, “LLM agent”, “autonomous agent”, “coding agent”, “browser agent”, “computer use agent”, and “MCP agent”, supplemented by curated project lists and snowballing from related repositories. A rerun of these queries on 2026-05-21 returned 5,852 summed raw hits before overlap removal and eligibility filtering. We then excluded repositories that did not satisfy three inclusion criteria: the project must integrate an LLM or model-compatible API, contain an executable entry point or package manifest, and expose at least one model-mediated action surface, such as tool calling, shell/process execution, file editing, browser automation, MCP/plugin integration, workflow execution, or persistent agent state. After applying these criteria, our final corpus contains 157 open-source LLM-based agent projects cloned from GitHub. The filtered manifest records each repository’s name, URL, local directory, analyzed commit, timestamps, project-purpose category, interface form, and star count. We treat the corpus as a fixed sample of popular agent applications, not an exhaustive census of all GitHub agent projects. Table I reports the distribution of agent categories. To systematically characterize repository-visible QA evidence, we first present the coding rubric and then describe the annotation procedure. The coding rubric consists of four analysis layers: execution surfaces , safeguards , testing artifacts , and risk scenarios . We use the rubric to turn repository artifacts into coded records that answer four operational questions. Execution-surface records identify the interfaces and action channels through which an agent can receive requests or affect external systems, following work on tool use and side-effecting agent environments [ 28 , 10 , 9 , 11 ] . Safeguard records identify controls that authorize, scope, monitor, or block agent actions, following prompt-injection and agent-security work on tool, browser, and policy boundaries [ 12 , 14 , 29 , 9 , 15 ] . Testing-artifact records identify tests, evaluations, benchmarks, and failure-oriented checks for agent behavior under tasks, tools, and environments [ 30 , 10 , 9 , 11 ] . Risk-scenario records identify situations where agent behavior may reach sensitive actions, assets, or persistent state and therefore require boundary review [ 12 , 14 , 29 , 9 , 11 , 22 , 24 , 15 ] ; they are not confirmed vulnerabilities. Before applying the coding rubric, reviewers first familiarized themselves with each repository by reading README files, project documentation, configuration files, and directory structure to understand the project purpose, agent workflow, supported tools, deployment model, and permission assumptions. Reviewers then inspected repository artifacts related to agent execution, including documentation, source code, configuration files, manifests, tests, examples, deployment artifacts, and CI workflows.These artifacts were then coded using the four-layer rubric, recording project purpose, execution surfaces, safeguards, testing artifacts, and risk-scenario candidates. Our annotation followed three guidelines informed by qualitative-analysis practices in empirical software engineering [ 32 , 33 ] . First, every label had to point to a repository-visible artifact. Second, capability and QA labels were allowed to co-exist but captured different properties of the artifact: shell, browser, MCP, or plugin access was coded as a capability, while approval prompts, permission checks, sandboxing, redaction, monitoring, or tests were coded as QA mechanisms associated with that capability. Third, QA labels record the presence of reviewable mechanisms or testing intent, not validated runtime effectiveness; for example, a sandbox setting or test path shows that the repository contains a relevant QA mechanism, but we do not claim that the mechanism prevents all corresponding failures in deployed use. We developed the label set through open coding and annotation cards. Reviewers first inspected a diverse subset of repositories and wrote cards for recurring behaviors, recording the repository, artifact/path, behavior summary, tentative layer, and uncertainty note. Related cards were grouped and refined into the final labels; for example, a plugin artifact could be an execution-surface record when it added a model-callable extension channel, a safeguard record when it implemented permission checks, or a risk-scenario record when it linked plugin authority to untrusted context. We organize the study around two research questions. RQ1 examines coded records across four analysis layers, and RQ2 identifies the QA problems that remain undercovered within and across those layers. RQ1: What visible QA practice appears in open-source LLM-based agent projects? To answer this question, we examine four QA layers: RQ1.1: QA Challenges and Practices at the Execution surfaces. How do projects expose, separate, document, or qualify the entry points and action channels through which agents can affect external systems? RQ1.2: QA Challenges and Practices at the Safeguards. What safeguards are visible for constraining, validating, or monitoring model-mediated behavior before it reaches sensitive actions? RQ1.3: QA Challenges and Practices at the Testing Layer. What testing and evaluation artifacts are visible through tests, benchmarks, reproduction paths, robustness checks, security tests, or failure-oriented paths? RQ1.4: QA Challenges and Practices in Risk scenarios. What recurring situations allow agent behavior to reach sensitive actions, assets, or persistent state? RQ2: What QA problems remain undercovered in current open-source LLM-based agent projects? This question identifies missing, fragmented, or weak QA coverage across the four layers, including gaps in end-to-end workflow validation, cross-interface safeguard consistency, robustness and security testing, environment-aware validation, and documentation of bounded actions and trusted assumptions. This section reports an evidence-led synthesis for the two research questions. The execution surface is where an agent can affect external systems. The QA for this layer is therefore not only whether a surface exists, but whether the project can keep those surfaces safe. We derived the QA challenges and QA-practice families through manual review of repository-visible model-to-action paths, configuration paths, tool interfaces, and controls attached to those paths. Table III summarizes the main types of QA challenges and QA practices projects use to address them; percentages in the third column use the QA-challenge project count as the denominator. Inconsistent control across overlapping action paths occurs when a project exposes several routes to similar authority, so a control on one route may not cover another route. For example, google-gemini/gemini-cli exposes CLI, shell, filesystem, browser, web, and MCP paths, which makes cross-path consistency a central QA challenge. Outbound network/API effects beyond the project boundary occur when model-mediated behavior can send data or trigger remote actions outside the repository. For example, CherryHQ/cherry-studio exposes outbound provider, MCP, search, browser, and local API channels. Credential leakage through configuration occurs when provider keys, OAuth stores, browser profiles, or MCP environment variables become reachable by tools or subprocesses. For example, google-gemini/gemini-cli supports configured MCP environments and provider settings that have to be kept away from logs and tool outputs. Workspace escape through file access occurs when file tools, downloads, skills, or hooks can read or write outside the intended workspace. For example, OpenHands/OpenHands has workspace, sandbox, plugin, hook, and persisted-setting paths around file access. Host process and environment modification through commands occurs when model-selected commands can change host process state, environment variables, or workspace contents. For example, openai/codex exposes shell execution paths whose authority depends on approval and sandbox mode. Extension-driven authority expansion occurs when MCP servers, plugins, or skills add new model-callable tools and local subprocesses. For example, aaif-goose/goose treats MCP extensions as a primary capability. Unreviewed runtime code execution occurs when configured tools, imported modules, JavaScript, Python snippets, or runtime-loaded plugins execute logic outside the fixed application path. For example, google-gemini/gemini-cli supports extension and MCP configuration that can alter the set of callable runtime capabilities. Browser session and cross-domain exposure occurs when browser automation can interact with signed-in sessions, page scripts, cookies, uploads, downloads, or domains. For example, browser-use/browser-use exposes browser navigation and page interaction over persistent browser state. Approval and authorization controls require an explicit grant before a route performs a high-authority action or exposes sensitive API state. For example, CherryHQ/cherry-studio protects sensitive local API routes with bearer authentication, while google-gemini/gemini-cli uses confirmation and trust modes around interactive actions. This practice addresses inconsistent control across overlapping action paths, outbound network/API effects, host process modification through commands, extension-driven authority expansion, and browser session exposure. Sandboxing and isolation mechanisms run actions inside a bounded workspace, container, or restricted execution mode so file writes, command effects, and runtime-loaded code are separated from the host. For example, OpenHands/OpenHands separates workspace state and sandbox execution, and openai/codex routes shell commands through sandbox policy. This practice addresses overlapping action paths, workspace escape through file access, host process modification, and unreviewed runtime code execution. Permission and policy controls encode rules about which actions, paths, tools, routes, or modes are allowed before execution. For example, 1Panel-dev/MaxKB uses token permissions and tool filtering around custom Python tools and generated MCP servers. This practice addresses network/API effects, credential leakage, filesystem boundaries, commands, extensions, dynamic code, and browser actions by putting the allowed action set into a reviewable policy layer. Secret management and redaction limit where credentials can be stored, inherited, logged, or returned through a model/tool path. For example, google-gemini/gemini-cli includes logging redaction and environment sanitization around tool and provider flows. This practice directly addresses credential leakage through configuration and also supports filesystem, plugin, dynamic-code, and browser-session challenges where secrets may be inherited or exposed. MCP/plugin registration and configuration makes extension points explicit by listing configured servers, tools, commands, or generated plugin interfaces. For example, aaif-goose/goose pairs MCP extension support with permission, confirmation, and server-auth mechanisms. This practice addresses extension-driven authority expansion and unreviewed runtime code execution, and it also helps review overlapping action paths when plugin tools duplicate shell, file, browser, or network authority. Browser and domain-scoping controls restrict which domains, pages, scripts, uploads, downloads, or session data a browser agent can use. For example, browser-use/browser-use includes allowed/prohibited domain settings, sensitive-data filtering, IP blocking, storage-state handling, and upload-path gating. This practice addresses browser session and cross-domain exposure, and it also reduces credential leakage and outbound network/API effects when signed-in pages or uploaded files contain sensitive data. The safeguard layer examines whether projects put clear limits around high-authority agent actions. The main potential issue is incomplete control coverage: a project may protect one route to shell, file, browser, plugin, or secret access while another route to similar authority is less clearly bounded. Table IV summarizes the main safeguard issues and the safeguard practice families projects use to address them. Privileged command execution needs approval and containment because model-selected commands can change host process state, environment variables, or workspace contents. For example, openai/codex exposes shell execution paths whose authority depends on approval and sandbox mode. File and workspace access needs boundary control because file tools, downloads, skills, or hooks can read or write outside the intended workspace. For example, OpenHands/OpenHands separates workspace state and sandbox execution, which makes the workspace boundary a central review point. Secrets and credentials need scoped handling because provider keys, OAuth tokens, browser profiles, and MCP environment variables can become reachable by tools, subprocesses, logs, or provider calls. For example, google-gemini/gemini-cli combines provider configuration and MCP environments with logging and redaction paths. Plugin and MCP authority needs extension control because plugins and MCP servers can add model-callable tools, local subprocesses, and inherited environment access. For example, aaif-goose/goose treats MCP/plugin support as a primary capability that expands the set of callable actions. Browser session access needs domain and data scoping because browser agents can interact with signed-in sessions, page scripts, downloads, uploads, cookies, or domains. For example, browser-use/browser-use exposes browser navigation and page interaction over browser state that may persist across tasks or domains. Approval and authorization controls require an explicit grant before privileged execution or access to sensitive state. For example, openai/codex routes shell commands through approval policy, and aaif-goose/goose uses confirmation and server-auth mechanisms around extension paths. This practice addresses privileged command execution, plugin/MCP authority, browser session access, and secrets or credentials that should not be exposed without authorization. Sandboxing and isolation mechanisms run actions inside a bounded workspace, container, or restricted execution mode so command effects, file writes, and runtime-loaded code are separated from the host. For example, OpenHands/OpenHands separates workspace state from sandbox execution, while openai/codex supports sandbox policy around shell execution. This practice addresses privileged command execution, file/workspace boundary control, secrets and credentials, and plugin or runtime paths that may inherit host authority. Permission and policy controls encode rules about which commands, files, tools, routes, or modes are allowed before execution. For example, 1Panel-dev/MaxKB uses token permissions and tool filtering around custom Python tools and generated MCP servers. This practice addresses command execution, file/workspace access, credential handling, plugin/MCP authority, and browser session access by making the allowed action set reviewable. Secret management and redaction limit where credentials can be stored, inherited, logged, or returned through a model/tool path. For example, google-gemini/gemini-cli includes logging redaction and environment sanitization around tool and provider flows. This practice directly addresses secrets and credentials, and it also supports file/workspace, plugin/MCP, command, and browser-session challenges where sensitive values can be inherited or exposed. MCP/plugin registration and configuration makes extension authority explicit by listing configured servers, tools, commands, or generated plugin interfaces. For example, aaif-goose/goose pairs MCP extension support with permission, confirmation, and server-auth mechanisms. This practice addresses plugin/MCP authority and helps review command, file, credential, and browser challenges introduced by extension-provided tools. Browser and domain-scoping controls restrict which domains, pages, scripts, uploads, downloads, or session data a browser agent can use. For example, browser-use/browser-use includes allowed/prohibited domain settings, sensitive-data filtering, IP blocking, storage-state handling, and upload-path gating. This practice addresses browser session access and also reduces credential exposure and file/upload risks when signed-in pages or local files contain sensitive data. Software testing itself is a conventional QA mechanism. From the repository review, we grouped testing artifacts into four testing-practice categories. Across the 157 projects, the counts are: 137 (87.3%) contain conventional tests or specs, 95 (60.5%) contain security/safety-oriented tests, 78 (49.7%) contain evaluation, benchmark, adversarial, or red-team-like paths, and 8 (5.1%) contain prompt-injection, adversarial, jailbreak, or red-team testing paths. Conventional tests and specs. These tests address ordinary implementation regressions in tool wrappers, API routes, storage, settings, UI helpers, provider clients, and parsers. They are useful because many agent failures still begin as ordinary software bugs: a tool argument is parsed incorrectly, a session setting is not persisted, or a file operation returns the wrong result. For example, OpenHands/OpenHands tests sandbox cleanup behavior, including no-sandbox cases, pagination, stale sandbox cleanup, pause failures, invalid cleanup limits, and sorting by creation time; it also tests secret-store initialization, serialization, provider-token handling, and frontend role-permission checks. browser-use/browser-use tests CLI sessions, filesystem integration, action-loop detection, coordinate clicking, browser navigation, and setup-command handling. Security/safety-oriented tests. These tests address boundary regressions around high-authority actions, especially shell execution, filesystem access, browser sessions, domain policy, secrets, approval, sandboxing, and tool permissions. They are more directly agent-specific because the failure condition is not just that a function returns the wrong value, but that an agent action crosses a boundary it should not cross. For example, browser-use/browser-use tests that prohibited domains are blocked, allowed-domain lists override broad access, authentication text in a URL does not bypass domain checks, private or localhost IP addresses can be blocked, password fields are removed from DOM snapshots, and sensitive values are filtered from action results. google-gemini/gemini-cli tests shell-safety cases such as preferring file-write tools over shell commands for file creation, avoiding destructive shell commands, recovering when sandbox permissions are insufficient, and masking long tool outputs before they are reused. Evaluation and red-team-like practices. These practices address behavior that only appears after the model chooses actions over one or more steps. They include task evals, benchmark runners, replayable response fixtures, adversarial prompts, and red-team scenarios. For example, google-gemini/gemini-cli uses evals for automated tool use, plan mode, subtask delegation, browser-agent workflows, background processes, memory behavior, and eval regression; these checks ask whether the agent chooses the expected tool sequence rather than only whether a helper function works. Alibaba-NLP/DeepResearch uses JSONL eval data and evaluation scripts for deep-search and web-agent workflows. cordum-io/cordum includes red-team scenarios that exercise approval, policy, tenant isolation, validation, and limit handling. Prompt-injection and adversarial tests. These tests address the potential issue that untrusted pages, files, prompts, skills, or MCP responses can steer the agent away from the user’s intent or policy. They are a specialized form of security/safety or red-team testing. For example, Yeachan-Heo/oh-my-claudecode tests that subagent prompts prepend a fixed system header, preserve the order of system, file, and user context, reject context file paths containing newlines, carriage returns, null bytes, or path traversal, and reject invalid agent-role names. NousResearch/hermes-agent includes prompt-injection and red-teaming tests around scheduled tools and bundled skills. The risk-scenario layer is organized around risk-chain templates. Here, the unit of analysis is the end-to-end path rather than the individual surface or control: behaviors that are ordinary in isolation, such as reading files, invoking tools, reusing state, loading extensions, or using browser sessions, may become risky when connected through model decisions or untrusted context before reaching a sensitive action or asset. Table V reports risk-chain QA challenges and the QA practices used in projects showing each chain. Secret-to-tool chain. A stored key, OAuth token, browser profile, or MCP environment variable becomes part of a model-mediated tool path and may then flow into logs, subprocesses, provider calls, or tool outputs. For example, google-gemini/gemini-cli combines MCP environments, tool arguments, errors, and provider-facing content, so the review question is whether secret scope is preserved across the whole path. Workspace-to-persistent-state chain. A model-selected file operation, hook, plugin, or subagent crosses from the task workspace into persisted settings, stored state, or secret storage. For example, OpenHands/OpenHands connects workspace state, settings, hooks, plugins, and secret storage, so the review question is whether the intended workspace boundary still holds after state is reused. Extension-to-authority chain. A configured plugin, MCP server, or skill adds a new model-callable action that inherits local subprocess, network, file, or environment authority. For example, aaif-goose/goose treats MCP extensions as first-class capabilities, so the review question is whether newly added tools inherit the same trust and permission assumptions as built-in tools. Mode-switch-to-privilege chain. An action that is checked in an interactive path is reachable through another mode, such as an automatic mode, setup hook, API route, headless path, or alternate tool. For example, openai/codex includes multiple shell-related modes and control paths, so the review question is whether the same privileged action remains bounded after the execution mode changes. Runtime-code chain. Configuration, imported modules, JavaScript, Python snippets, or runtime-loaded plugins introduce executable logic after the fixed application code has been reviewed. For example, google-gemini/gemini-cli combines extension and MCP configuration with runtime capability changes, so the review question is whether loaded code is subject to the same review boundary as built-in code. Model-to-process chain. A model-selected action reaches a host process, environment variable, background job, or workspace mutation. For example, openai/codex exposes command execution through more than one control path, so the review question is whether command authority is bounded at the action level rather than only at one interface. Session-to-action chain. Browser state, cookies, storage, uploads, downloads, or signed-in pages persist across domains or tasks and later influence an agent action. For example, browser-use/browser-use connects navigation, page interaction, storage state, and uploads, so the review question is whether session state remains scoped to the intended task and domain. Untrusted-context-to-action chain. A page, file, prompt, tool output, or MCP response influences a later tool call, command, file operation, or data disclosure. For example, Yeachan-Heo/oh-my-claudecode handles subagent context files, so the review question is whether untrusted context can move from input material into later privileged actions. QA practices in this layer can be grouped into two broad categories. Chain-interruption practices stop a risky path at a critical transition point, such as when a model-mediated workflow reaches a privileged action, host execution, or sensitive data. Authorize the transition to a privileged action. Approval and authorization controls interrupt a chain when a model-mediated path reaches a sensitive action. This practice appears in 137 of 149 secret-to-tool chains, 129 of 137 extension-to-authority chains, 114 of 123 mode-switch-to-privilege chains, 123 of 131 model-to-process chains, 53 of 60 session-to-action chains, and 39 of 45 untrusted-context-to-action chains. For example, openai/codex uses an approval policy around command execution paths, and aaif-goose/goose uses confirmation and server-auth mechanisms around extension paths. Contain execution or state effects. Sandboxing and isolation mechanisms interrupt a chain by preventing a tool, command, runtime module, or workspace operation from inheriting unrestricted host authority. This practice appears in 104 of 149 secret-to-tool chains, 90 of 128 workspace-to-persistent-state chains, 84 of 123 mode-switch-to-privilege chains, 73 of 99 runtime-code chains, and 91 of 131 model-to-process chains. For example, OpenHands/OpenHands separates workspace state from sandbox execution, while openai/codex applies sandbox policy to shell execution. Stop secret propagation. Secret management and redaction interrupt a chain by preventing credentials from being inherited, logged, returned through tool output, or sent into provider-facing content. This practice appears in 96 of 149 secret-to-tool chains, 82 of 128 workspace-to-persistent-state chains, 91 of 137 extension-to-authority chains, 84 of 131 model-to-process chains, 38 of 60 session-to-action chains, and 25 of 45 untrusted-context-to-action chains. For example, google-gemini/gemini-cli includes logging redaction and environment sanitization around tool and provider flows. Systematic risk-avoidance practices reduce the chance that such a path forms in the first place by limiting risky combinations. Scope allowed paths, tools, modes, and data flows. Permission and policy controls avoid risky chains by making the allowed action set explicit before execution. This practice appears in 100 of 149 secret-to-tool chains, 84 of 128 workspace-to-persistent-state chains, 94 of 137 extension-to-authority chains, 82 of 123 mode-switch-to-privilege chains, 69 of 99 runtime-code chains, 91 of 131 model-to-process chains, 44 of 60 session-to-action chains, and 27 of 45 untrusted-context-to-action chains. For example, 1Panel-dev/MaxKB uses token permissions and tool filtering around custom Python tools and generated MCP servers. Make extension and runtime authority reviewable. MCP/plugin registration and configuration avoid hidden authority chains by making added tools, servers, commands, or generated interfaces visible before they become model-callable. This practice appears in 101 of 137 extension-to-authority chains and 75 of 99 runtime-code chains. For example, aaif-goose/goose exposes MCP extension configuration as a primary control point. Scope browser sessions and domains. Browser and domain-scoping controls avoid session-to-action chains by limiting which pages, domains, uploads, downloads, storage state, or signed-in sessions can influence later actions. This practice appears in 50 of 60 session-to-action chains and 24 of 45 untrusted-context-to-action chains. For example, browser-use/browser-use includes domain restrictions, sensitive-data filtering, storage-state handling, and upload-path controls. This RQ examines which QA problems remain undercovered across the four RQ1 layers. We treat a problem as undercovered when repositories expose the problem but lack the most directly relevant QA practice, or when the corresponding practice is implemented only as a local control for a specific route, mode, or artifact type rather than as systematic coverage. Table VI summarizes the largest direct gaps by RQ1 dimension. Execution surfaces. The table shows that the weakest coverage is not for obscure surfaces, but for common routes such as credentials, network/API calls, file access, shell commands, and dynamic code. In these cases, the project exposes an action route but lacks the direct control expected for that route. For example, vercel-labs/agent-browser is counted in the credential gap because its review record includes environment secrets, browser state, injected headers, and cloud profiles reachable from browser/CLI paths, while it does not match the secret-management/redaction practice rule. 0x4m4/hexstrike-ai is counted in the file and command gaps because its review record links user/model-controlled paths and shell commands to API/MCP routes, while the corresponding sandbox/isolation practice is not present under our rule. The practical implication is that surface inventory alone is insufficient; each action route needs an attached boundary such as redaction, permission policy, or sandboxing. Safeguards. The safeguard gaps show that broad controls do not always cover the specific action that needs protection. Secret handling, workspace containment, MCP/plugin extension, and browser session control need different direct practices, but projects often rely on more general approval/authentication or configuration assumptions. For example, multica-ai/multica is counted in the MCP/plugin gap because its review record describes stored per-agent MCP configuration being passed to Claude Code as a local tool channel, but it lacks the direct MCP/plugin registration practice under our reproducible rule. 0x4m4/hexstrike-ai is counted in the browser/domain gap because its browser agent can visit arbitrary URLs and return browser-observed secrets, but no browser/domain-scoping control is matched. The remaining QA gap is therefore not simply “add a safeguard”; it is to bind the right safeguard to the specific sensitive action. Testing artifacts. The testing gaps are the most direct sign that QA practice has not caught up with agent-specific failure modes. Projects may have ordinary tests, but the missing direct practices are adversarial tests for untrusted context, replay/regression tests for multi-step behavior, and security/safety tests for high-authority actions. For example, browser-use/browser-use is counted in the untrusted-context testing gap because its review record links model-reachable browser JavaScript execution and browser-domain policy defaults to prompt-injection-style risk, while it does not match the prompt-injection/adversarial test rule. reworkd/AgentGPT is similarly counted because external snippets are inserted into summarization prompts, but the matching adversarial test practice is absent. The remaining gap is failure sensitivity: tests should fail when a model-mediated action escapes an approval, sandbox, credential, plugin, file, or browser boundary. Risk scenarios. The risk-scenario gaps identify chains that need to be converted into QA requirements. These chains include credential flow into tools or subprocesses, commands affecting host state, workspace-boundary crossing, extension-based authority, and runtime-loaded code. For example, Fosowl/agenticSeek is counted in the credential-flow gap because its review record links LLM-generated Python execution to backend secrets, while secret-management/redaction is not matched. 0x4m4/hexstrike-ai is counted in the command-execution gap because an unauthenticated API route can reach host shell execution, while sandbox/isolation is not matched. The remaining gap is operationalization: each chain should name the trigger, protected asset, required control, and regression check that would stop the chain. Recommendations. First, projects should define controls by protected action or asset rather than by interface, so the same secret, file, shell, plugin, browser, and network boundary applies across CLI, API, MCP, browser, headless, and batch routes. Second, each high-authority route or risk chain should have a failure-oriented test or replay case that fails when the required approval, sandbox, policy, redaction, domain scope, or extension check is removed. Internal validity. Our analysis is based on repository-level artifacts, including source code, documentation, configuration, tests, and structured review notes. This view captures what developers make inspectable in the repository, but may not include hosted services, provider-side controls, deployment-specific settings, or dependency behavior outside the inspected snapshot. Automated search and LLM-assisted summarization helped identify the candidate artifacts, but may introduce false positives, false negatives, or inconsistent terminology. We mitigate this risk through manual verification of candidate artifacts and a fixed coding schema for quantitative analysis. Because of objective was to inductively develop a repository-level coding framework through iterative open coding, the coding categories evolved during analysis instead of using a fixed predefined codebook. Consequently, we did not compute inter-rater agreement during taxonomy construction. To improve consistency, reviewers continuously refined label definitions, discussed ambiguous cases, and resolved disagreements through consensus before applying the finalized coding rubric across the corpus. This approach follows common qualitative coding practices used for inductive taxonomy development in empirical software engineering. [ 34 , 35 ] . Construct validity. The four analysis layers provide an operational coding rubric rather than a universal taxonomy of agent QA. Some projects could reasonably be grouped differently, especially when one artifact plays multiple roles, such as exposing a tool, constraining its use, and documenting a risk scenario. To reduce this ambiguity, we separated capabilities from QA mechanisms and kept structured records for paths, labels, and review notes. Our counts should be read as repository-visible QA practices, not as measurements of runtime effectiveness. External validity. The corpus is a fixed May 2026 snapshot of popular open-source GitHub projects and overrepresents coding and browser/computer-use agents. It is not a census of all agent repositories; closed-source, enterprise, and small prototype agents may differ. GitHub stars are descriptive metadata, not a security-maturity measure, and repositories may have changed after collection. This paper presented an empirical study of 157 open-source LLM-based agent projects. Using a four-layer coding rubric, we characterized execution surfaces, safeguards, testing artifacts, and risk scenarios from repository artifacts and coded records. The results show that QA practices are common, but their coverage across agent workflows remains uneven. The main gap is not whether projects contain QA artifacts, but whether those artifacts cover the full agent workflow. Future agent QA should make tool authority explicit, connect safeguards and tests to the situations where sensitive actions are reached, and add failure-oriented checks for boundary, adversarial, and multi-step tool-use cases.

sources.text: Front. Comput. Sci. , 28 August 2026 Sec. Software Volume 8 - 2026 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fcomp.2026.1936730 Randa Ouaarous 1 * Imane Hilal 2 Abdellatif Mezrioui 1 1. STRS Lab/CEDOC 2TI, Institut National des Postes et des Telecommunications (INPT), Rabat, Morocco 2. ITQAN Team, LyRica Lab, Information Sciences School (ESI), Rabat, Morocco Article metrics The growing complexity of software systems has increased demand for intelligent solutions in Software Quality Assurance (SQA). Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers autonomous decision-making, adaptive behavior, and proactive quality improvement, yet its applications across SQA remain fragmented. This systematic mapping study examines Agentic AI integration in SQA, analyzing application distribution, agent characteristics, and supported stakeholder roles to identify coverage, trends, benefits, limitations, and gaps. Following systematic mapping protocols and PRISMA, five digital libraries were searched, retrieving 37 primary studies. Data were classified through frequency analysis and qualitative categorization aligned with Agentic AI behavior, architecture, and autonomy dimensions. Applications concentrate in Product Assurance, mainly test generation and defect management, with fewer studies in Process or Planning activities. Most agents exhibit goal-oriented or diagnostic behaviors, moderate autonomy, and hybrid or multi-agent architectures. Benefits include efficiency, accuracy, and maintainability improvements; limitations involve scalability, generalizability, and transparency. Role coverage focuses on execution-level stakeholders, while managerial and leadership roles receive minimal support. Agentic AI shows potential for strengthening SQA intelligence and adaptability but remains unevenly distributed across activities and roles. Transparency, validation, and leadership support are priority research gaps for developing trustworthy, process-aware Agentic systems across the full SQA lifecycle. Software Engineering emerged in the 1960s as a discipline within computer science, focusing on the systematic development of software systems ( Batarseh et al., 2020 ). Today, software engineering plays a pivotal role across multiple sectors, including IT-services, finance/insurance, manufacturing and software publishing, which represent the top industries employing software engineers ( U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024 ). However, software systems, which are human-designed artifacts, are prone to defects. Such defects can have severe consequences, potentially endangering business operations, compromising resources, or even threatening human lives ( ISTQB, 2024 ). To mitigate these risks, Software Quality Assurance (SQA) has become an indispensable component of the Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC), aiming to ensure that software meets the quality requirements defined by stakeholders ( Zhao et al., 2021 ). Over the past decades, SQA has expanded in scope and complexity alongside the evolution of software engineering. This growth has introduced new challenges, including the need to align quality practices with diverse organizational structures and constraints, as well as the high costs associated with comprehensive SQA activities ( Zhang et al., 2024 ). Moreover, the accelerating pace of technological change demands continuous innovation in SQA practices. Methodologies such as Agile and DevOps, with their emphasis on rapid delivery, can reduce the involvement of QA in early development phases ( Bhanushali, 2023 ), potentially delaying defect detection and increasing the cost and complexity of remediation. Effective communication and collaboration in such fast-paced environments are equally challenging ( Almashhadani et al., 2023 ). The adoption of continuous integration (CI) and continuous testing (CT) further compounds these difficulties, as teams must manage frequent code changes and maintain the reliability of automated testing pipelines ( Bhanushali, 2023 ; Shuib and Hassan, 2021 ). In parallel, contemporary software systems increasingly operate in highly dynamic and heterogeneous environments, such as Internet of Things (IoT) platforms, cyber-physical systems, and large-scale distributed architectures. These environments are characterized by continuous evolution, frequent configuration changes, and increasingly complex interactions between software, data, and physical components. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is also experiencing rapid advancements and is increasingly applied to address these challenges in SQA. Recent industry reports indicate that 71% of organizations have adopted AI in some capacity, with 34% actively leveraging it for SQA ( Capgemini and Sogeti, 2024 ). Among the emerging AI paradigms, Agentic AI has attracted particular attention because of its ability to autonomously pursue goals, adapt to changing environments, and execute complex tasks with reduced human intervention ( Guenat et al., 2022 ). Unlike traditional AI systems, which are generally designed for predefined prediction or classification tasks, and generative AI systems, which primarily focus on content generation, Agentic AI combines reasoning, planning, and adaptive decision-making to achieve goals through autonomous action ( Acharya et al., 2025 ). Despite this growing momentum, the adoption of Agentic AI across Software Quality Assurance remains fragmented and uneven. Existing studies primarily focus on operational activities, particularly software testing, while planning, process assurance, and leadership support receive considerably less attention. Furthermore, long-term industrial validation and discussions of explainability, accountability, data quality, and ethical considerations remain limited. As noted by Kokol (2024) , AI research in software engineering is still spread across fragmented initiatives rather than coherent research frameworks. Consequently, researchers and practitioners still lack a consolidated understanding of how Agentic AI is transforming the Software Quality Assurance lifecycle, where adoption is most mature, and which areas remain insufficiently explored. To address this gap, this paper presents a systematic mapping study (SMS) of Agentic AI in Software Quality Assurance. Unlike a systematic literature review, which synthesizes evidence to answer narrowly focused research questions, an SMS provides a structured overview of research trends, thematic distribution, and knowledge gaps across an emerging field. By systematically classifying and mapping the selected studies, this work identifies how Agentic AI is being adopted across SQA activities, characterizes the implemented agents according to their behavior, architecture, and autonomy, and examines the stakeholder roles they support. Collectively, these analyses provide a comprehensive picture of the current landscape of Agentic AI in SQA, highlighting adoption patterns, research maturity, and opportunities for future research. The study is guided by three research questions: RQ1. How are Agentic AI applications distributed across SQA activities, and what agent characteristics are associated with each activity? RQ2. What categories of benefits and limitations are reported across Agentic AI applications in SQA, and how do they co-occur? RQ3. Which SQA roles are supported by Agentic AI systems, and what gaps in role coverage exist? The structure of this paper is as follows. Section 2 introduces the background concepts of SQA and Agentic AI. Section 3 reviews related work on the use of AI in SQA to situate this study within the existing body of literature. Section 4 describes the mapping methodology, including the search strategy, selection criteria, and data extraction procedures. Section 5 presents the analysis, results, and findings of the mapping. Section 6 discusses the implications of these findings, including benefits, limitations, and supported SQA roles. Section 7 lists the threats to validity of this study. Finally, Section 8 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research. To structure the analysis of Agentic AI applications, this study adopts a taxonomy that organizes SQA into three main categories: SQA Planning, SQA Process Assurance, and SQA Product Assurance. Each category contains sub-activities that represent important quality assurance practices across the software lifecycle. This taxonomy is based on well-established standards such as the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge (SWEBOK v4.0) ( Washizaki, 2024 ) and the ISTQB Syllabus ( ISTQB, 2024 ). These sources define SQA not as a single process, but as a set of related tasks distributed across planning, process conformance, and product validation. The taxonomy is illustrated in Figure 1 . Figure 1 Taxonomy of software quality assurance activities showing the three categories and associated sub-activities. SQA Planning covers early quality-related activities in a software project. It includes: QA Strategy Definition: defining quality objectives, identifying quality characteristics, and selecting assurance techniques. QA Effort Estimation: forecasting resources and time needed for SQA tasks. QA Risk Management: identifying and mitigating risks that can affect quality outcomes. Quality Standards Definition: selecting applicable standards (e.g., ISO/IEC 25010) and guidelines for conformance. These activities align with SWEBOK’s Software Quality and Software Engineering Management knowledge areas, especially quality planning and management ( Washizaki, 2024 ). SQA Process Assurance ensures that software development and maintenance processes are defined, followed, and continuously improved. It includes: Compliance to Processes: auditing and assessing adherence to predefined processes (e.g., ISO/IEC 12207, CMMI). Configuration Management: managing changes and baselines for software artifacts. People Skill Management: ensuring that teams have the competence and training needed to perform SQA effectively. These sub-activities map to SWEBOK’s Software Engineering Process knowledge area and ISTQB’s process-oriented quality attributes ( Washizaki, 2024 ; ISTQB, 2024 ). SQA Product Assurance verifies that the software product meets requirements through direct evaluation. It includes: Requirement Review: checking requirements for clarity, consistency, and testability. Design Review: evaluating architectural and detailed design artifacts against standards and requirements. Software Testing: performing static and dynamic testing to detect defects and assess quality attributes such as functionality, performance, and security. This dimension corresponds to the Verification and Validation and Software Testing knowledge areas in SWEBOK, and to the test process, test design, and test execution practices defined by ISTQB ( Washizaki, 2024 ; ISTQB, 2024 ). Artificial Intelligence has evolved from rule-based and predictive systems toward generative models and, more recently, toward autonomous systems capable of pursuing complex objectives with limited human intervention. This evolution has given rise to Agentic AI, an emerging paradigm that extends AI capabilities beyond content generation by integrating reasoning, planning, memory, tool use, and adaptive decision-making to execute multi-step tasks autonomously ( Sibai et al., 2026 ). Within Software Engineering, this evolution reflects a broader transition from AI-assisted development tools toward increasingly autonomous systems capable of supporting complex software engineering activities and collaborating with human developers throughout the software lifecycle ( Nguyen-Duc et al., 2025 ). Informed by established definitions of intelligent agents and recent Agentic AI surveys ( Acharya et al., 2025 ; Russell and Norvig, 2021 ; Jennings et al., 1998 ; Franklin and Graesser, 1997 ; Jennings, 2000 ), Agentic AI is operationalized in this study as an AI system that (i) maintains explicit goals related to quality outcomes, (ii) autonomously selects and sequences actions to achieve these goals, and (iii) adapts its behavior based on feedback from the software and its environment. This operational definition provides a consistent basis for identifying and classifying the primary studies included in this systematic mapping study. The distinction between Agentic AI and previous AI paradigms is important. Traditional AI primarily supports prediction, classification, or optimization tasks, while generative AI focuses on producing new content from learned patterns. Building on these capabilities, Agentic AI pursues complex objectives through autonomous or semi-autonomous execution ( Sibai et al., 2026 ). These capabilities enable Agentic systems to coordinate multiple actions, interact with external tools, and continuously adapt their strategies according to changing environments and user objectives. These characteristics are particularly relevant to Software Quality Assurance, where activities such as software testing, quality assessment, compliance monitoring, defect analysis, and risk management require continuous adaptation to evolving software artifacts and development environments. These perspectives were selected because goal-directed behavior, agent organization, and degree of autonomy represent recurring properties in established agent research ( Russell and Norvig, 2021 ; Jennings et al., 1998 ; Franklin and Graesser, 1997 ; Jennings, 2000 ) and recent Agentic AI literature ( Acharya et al., 2025 ). Building on these advances, Agentic AI offers the potential to support more autonomous, context-aware, and goal-driven Software Quality Assurance processes. To analyze the selected studies consistently, this research characterizes each Agentic AI system according to three complementary perspectives: behavior, architecture, and autonomy. These perspectives were selected because they represent recurring characteristics reported across the reviewed literature and provide a consistent analytical lens for comparing heterogeneous Agentic AI implementations across different Software Quality Assurance activities. They are intended as analytical dimensions for this mapping study rather than as a universal taxonomy of Agentic AI. To identify studies for the related-work comparison, a complementary search was conducted in November 2025. The search combined terms related to artificial intelligence, generative AI, Agentic AI, and large language models with terms related to Software Quality Assurance, software testing, review, survey, mapping, and taxonomy. Reviews, surveys, taxonomies, and broad research contributions were retained when they synthesized prior work on AI in Software Engineering, SQA, or software testing and allowed comparison in terms of scope, contribution, and research gaps. Primary empirical studies without a literature synthesis and studies outside Software Engineering or software quality were excluded. Candidate publications were screened based on their title, abstract, and full text before inclusion in Table 1 . Several recent studies have examined how artificial intelligence is shaping software engineering and quality as presented in Table 1 . Hnatushenko and Pavlenko (2024) looked specifically at generative AI, noting its potential for automating test creation and detecting defects. Their focus, however, stayed narrowly on generative techniques and did not engage with broader Agentic properties. Ding (2024) offered a review of AI in testing for emerging domains and described several applications and developments, but the work was largely descriptive and lacked a systematic approach. Trifunova et al. (2024) also pointed to the transformative impact of AI in a short conference paper, though their study was brief and not comprehensive. On a broader level, Durrani et al. (2024) surveyed AI in software engineering across phases and activities between 2013 and 2023. While this provided a useful decade-long overview, the emphasis remained on the discipline, with little attention to SQA as a distinct activity. Hamid and Ali (2025) focused more narrowly on the effects of AI in software testing, especially in terms of efficiency and accuracy, but their analysis drew on a limited range of sources. By 2025, a series of preprints had begun to extend the discussion. Patil (2025) , for example, explored how large language models could be aligned with SQA standards. Shimmi et al. (2025) surveyed AI-driven techniques for vulnerability detection, while Pysmennyi et al. (2025) examined the growing landscape of AI tools in SQA, though their emphasis was mainly on cataloguing technologies. At the same time, a taxonomy study ( Schieferdecker, 2025 ) organized AI-augmented testing approaches, though its scope was intentionally limited to Software Testing rather than the full range of SQA activities. Taken together, these works show that the application of AI in SQA is becoming more sophisticated. Still, one gap is clear: Agentic properties, such as autonomy, behavior, and architecture, are rarely addressed in a systematic way. They are often hinted at but not explicitly connected to the established triad of SQA activities. To address this gap, the following sections introduce a systematic mapping protocol and an analytical classification framework that maps Agentic AI properties across SQA activities, providing a structured overview of research distribution, coverage, and gaps across the field. This study follows established guidelines for systematic mapping studies in software engineering, as outlined by Petersen et al. (2008) , whose methodology emphasizes structured classification, frequency analysis, and research landscape visualization to identify coverage gaps and distribution patterns across an emerging field. Elements of the search strategy and selection process follow Kitchenham and Charters (2007) , whose guidelines ensure transparency, rigor, and replicability in systematic studies. To structure the identification and screening process, the PRISMA framework was additionally applied ( Page et al., 2021 ), which provides reporting standards for systematic identification and selection of primary studies. The PRISMA process ( PRISMA, 2020 ) structures the review into four stages: identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion. In the identification stage, records are retrieved from selected databases and registers, with duplicates removed before screening. During screening, titles and abstracts are reviewed to exclude irrelevant works. In the eligibility stage, full-text reports are assessed against predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Finally, studies that meet all criteria are included in the review. This stepwise process is summarized in the PRISMA flowchart ( Supplementary Figure S1 ). This mapping is structured around three research questions that guided the search, selection, and synthesis process: RQ1: “How are Agentic AI applications distributed across SQA activities, and what agent characteristics are associated with each activity?” RQ2: “What categories of benefits and limitations are reported across Agentic AI applications in SQA, and how do they co-occur?” RQ3: “Which SQA roles are supported by Agentic AI systems, and what gaps in role coverage exist?” To ensure transparency, Table 2 maps each research question to the corresponding data items extracted from the primary studies and the analysis methods applied. This mapping provides traceability between the review objectives and the synthesis process. Table 2 Mapping of research questions to data items and analysis methods. To capture relevant studies, a multi-step search strategy was developed combining domain-specific keywords with Boolean operators across five digital libraries: IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, Scopus, SpringerLink, and ScienceDirect. IEEE Xplore and ACM Digital Library provide domain-specific coverage of software engineering and agent-based systems. Scopus served as a multidisciplinary aggregator with citation tracking, reducing publication bias and supporting cross-disciplinary retrieval. SpringerLink and ScienceDirect captured high-impact journals not fully indexed in conference-oriented repositories. Overlaps were managed through duplicate removal during identification. The final database searches were conducted in November 2025. The eligibility period covered studies published from January 2023 to the date of the final search in November 2025. The search string was designed to reflect both the terminology of Agentic AI systems and the scope of SQA: (“Agentic AI” OR “AI Agent” OR “AI Assistant” OR “Agentic RAG” OR “AI Chatbot” OR “Autonomous Agent” OR “Multi-Agent system”)) AND (“Software Quality” OR “Quality Assurance” OR “Software Testing” OR “Software Process Assurance” OR “Software Product Assurance”). The first clause covers expressions used for autonomous or semi-autonomous AI systems, including formal terms and practical instances. The second clause targets SQA constructs, from broad terms to specific activities. Before executing the final database searches, the search string was iteratively refined through exploratory searches using the studies identified in the authors’ previous systematic literature review on Agentic AI ( Ouaarous et al., 2024 ) as seed papers. These representative studies were used to verify that the selected keywords and their combinations consistently retrieved relevant literature across the selected databases while minimizing unrelated results. The seed papers were used solely to refine and validate the search strategy and were subsequently subjected to the same screening and eligibility criteria as all other retrieved records. To maintain rigor, predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied systematically during the selection process. These criteria ensured that only recent, peer-reviewed, and directly relevant studies were considered, while works lacking methodological detail or falling outside the scope of Agentic AI in SQA were excluded. A summary of the applied criteria is presented in Table 3 . Table 3 Inclusion and exclusion criteria applied for this SMS. The time window from 2023 to 2025 was selected deliberately to capture the emergence of Agentic AI as a distinct paradigm, which became prominent following advances in large language models and autonomous agent frameworks. Earlier studies on agent-based systems were excluded when they did not explicitly address agent autonomy in quality assurance contexts. This temporal focus prioritizes conceptual relevance over historical completeness. The studies that satisfied these conditions proceeded to the screening and selection stages, as described in Section 4.6. Following the PRISMA stages described in Section 4.1, selection proceeded through automated duplicate/non-accessible entry removal, title-and-abstract screening, relevance-based abstract review, and full-text review against the inclusion and exclusion criteria in Table 3 . Quality was further assessed based on methodological rigor, clarity of findings, and relevance to the research questions. The PRISMA flowchart in Figure 2 documents the selection process for the present study. Figure 2 PRISMA flowchart illustrating the study selection process in this paper. For each study that passed the selection process, a structured data extraction form was used to collect consistent information. The form was designed and piloted on a small subset of papers to ensure clarity and completeness before being applied to the entire dataset. The following categories were extracted: Bibliographic information: title, authors, year, venue. Study context: domain of application, type of system under test (traditional software, AI/ML system, IoT, etc.). SQA activity: planning, process assurance, or product assurance, with sub-activities such as requirement review, design review, or software testing. Agentic AI characteristics: any description of Agentic AI used Roles supported: stakeholder roles assisted by the system (e.g., developer, QA, QA lead). Outcomes: reported benefits, limitations, or challenges. Research gaps or future directions identified by the authors. Extraction was performed independently by three reviewers to reduce bias, with disagreements resolved through discussion. Data were recorded in a shared spreadsheet to enable traceability and verification. The extracted data were classified and mapped using both quantitative and qualitative approaches, following the systematic mapping study protocol of Petersen et al. (2008) . A descriptive mapping was first performed to report frequencies and distributions, such as the number of studies per year, by SQA activity, or by type of Agentic AI applied. This provided a structured overview of research coverage, publication trends, and concentration patterns across the field. To enable consistent interpretation and visualization, extracted benefits, limitations, and assisted roles were categorized through an inductive classification process. The categories emerged from iterative coding of the primary studies and were refined until stable category boundaries were established. The resulting mapping tables ( Supplementary Tables S2–S4 ) summarize the classification scheme and the distribution of each category across studies. These tables are provided in Supplementary materials to ensure transparency and reproducibility of the mapping process. To address the research questions systematically, the mapping was organized as follows: RQ1 was addressed by classifying and mapping studies to SQA activities, SQA sub-activities, and agent characteristics to reveal distribution patterns and coverage gaps. RQ2 was addressed by classifying reported benefits and limitations into categories, calculating their relative frequencies, and analyzing their co-occurrence patterns. RQ3 was addressed by mapping the distribution of supported roles across autonomy levels and identifying underrepresented stakeholder categories. Finally, cross-analysis was performed to map SQA activities against Agentic AI properties and identify coverage gaps. Rayyan was used to manage duplicate checking and the screening of candidate studies. Microsoft Excel was used to maintain the review protocol, record screening decisions, and organize the extraction and classification tables. Quantitative analysis and visualization were conducted in R version 4.5.1 through RStudio 2025.09.0 + 387. The ggplot2 package was used to generate the distribution charts, frequency matrices, and bubble chart; reshape2 was used to restructure the cross-tabulated data; and igraph was used to construct the benefit-limitation co-occurrence network. The manuscript tables were produced from the validated Excel classification sheets. The final dataset consisted of 37 primary studies published between 2023 and 2025, forming the research map analyzed in the following sections. To analyze the selected studies in a structured manner, a classification lens was developed to combines perspectives from both Agentic AI and SQA. After reviewing the literature, three recurring dimensions of Agentic AI were identified that could be consistently applied across the included studies. These dimensions are also grounded in established agent research ( Russell and Norvig, 2021 ; Jennings et al., 1998 ; Franklin and Graesser, 1997 ; Jennings, 2000 ). The focus was specifically on behavior, architecture, and autonomy because they capture the operational characteristics of agents that are most relevant for SQA. Other properties discussed in agent literature, such as social ability or mobility, are less central to quality assurance tasks, whereas behavior, architecture, and autonomy directly affect how agents can support planning, process assurance, and product assurance activities. This focus allows the review to connect established agent concepts with concrete SQA practices. The framework does not prescribe causal relationships but serves as an analytical lens to classify and compare existing studies. This subsection presents the application of Agentic AI across SQA activities, following the taxonomy introduced in Section 3.1 and the classification framework in Section 5.2. The analysis is structured by the three main SQA activities, planning, process assurance, and product assurance, and further divided into their sub-activities. In this mapping study, SQA activities are classified according to the nature of the evaluated object rather than the organizational phase in which the activity occurs. Activities that directly assess software artifacts, such as requirements review and design review are categorized under SQA Product Assurance, even when they are embedded within development or governance processes. Accordingly, requirements validation and refinement are treated as product assurance activities, as they evaluate the quality, consistency, and testability of requirements artifacts. This interpretation follows the SWEBOK distinction between process conformance and product evaluation and is applied consistently throughout the analysis. For each sub-activity, the number of relevant studies is reported ( Figure 6 ), summarize representative contributions, and highlight the Agentic AI dimensions observed. From the 37 primary studies, seven focused on SQA Planning. These studies were divided between QA strategy definition (2), QA effort estimation (2), QA risk management (1), and quality standards definition (2). Most of the systems used goal-oriented or workflow optimization behaviors. Their autonomy was between copilot and adaptive, and the architecture was either monolithic or hierarchical. Agentic AI applications in SQA Planning mainly supported QA strategy definition and effort estimation, while considerably less attention was devoted to QA risk management and quality standards definition. Studies on strategy definition demonstrated improvements in quality planning and coverage enhancement, although scalability and reasoning accuracy remained important challenges. Similarly, effort estimation applications reported productivity and cost benefits but showed reduced accuracy when applied to unfamiliar project contexts. Evidence for risk management was limited to a single conceptual framework addressing quality assurance for AI-intensive systems, whereas quality standards definition focused on adaptive compliance monitoring using MAPE-K-based multi-agent architectures. Overall, the available evidence suggests that Agentic AI is currently used to support planning decisions rather than to automate strategic quality management, reflecting the need for continued human oversight in planning activities. Agentic AI applications in SQA Process Assurance predominantly focused on compliance to processes, with six studies addressing activities such as Agile sprint planning ( Khan and Daviglus, 2025 ), TDD/CI-CD workflows ( Atul et al., 2024 ), compliance auditing ( Hilario et al., 2024 ; Waltersdorfer and Sabou, 2025 ), and requirement validation in global software development ( Ramasamy et al., 2024 ; Rauf et al., 2023 ). Across these application contexts, the reported benefits consistently included improved productivity, traceability, and compliance assurance, while recurring limitations related to validation, reliability, and reasoning accuracy suggest that these challenges are inherent to current LLM-based reasoning rather than specific to individual process activities. While these studies indicate that Agentic AI could also support broader process-oriented assurance activities, the available evidence remains preliminary, highlighting that current research continues to prioritize operational process compliance over organizational capability development. Reported systems displayed goal-oriented, generative, diagnostic, and workflow optimization behaviors, with autonomy ranging from copilot to autopilot and adaptive, and architectures spanning monolithic, multi-agent, and hierarchical orchestration.
